text:
Saskatchewan Supreme Court

[TRIAL]

Citation: Jones v. Jones

Date: 1925-01-24

Divorce—Cruelty—Mental Distress and Injury to Health.

Where the conduct of a husband in obliging his wife to earn
her own living while he spends his earnings on a mistress for whom he openly
indicates his preference so preys on the wife’s mind that, to his knowledge, it
undermines her health, it constitutes that cruelty which, coupled with
adultery, entitles her to a divorce, even though he has not been physically
violent towards her.

The finding of fact as to whether the wife’s health was
injured or is menaced must be made in the light of the common knowledge of
today as to the effect of misery and anguish of mind on the sufferer’s health,
each case being considered on its own special facts. The character, whether
assertive, bold, or sensitive, the degree of refinement, physical well-being,
condition of health, mental and bodily, means of living, position in society
and previous training are all relevant to the determination.

Authorities exhaustively reviewed in chronological order and
held to point to a breaking away in all Courts from the rigour of the decisions
on the subject in the Ecclesiastical Courts.
(Beauclerk v. Beauclerk
[1891]
P. 189, 60 L.J.P.C. 20 referred to as the case nearest in point to the present
case, and applied).

This was an action by the plaintiff (wife) against the
defendant (husband) for dissolution of marriage on the ground of adultery,
coupled with cruelty and for alimony. The action was tried before
Taylor,
J., without a jury and judgment
was given the plaintiff for a decree
nisi,
six months, with costs and
with leave to apply again for alimony.

Council:

J
.
Cairns,
for plaintiff.

Defendants not appearing.

[
1
]

TAYLOR
,
J. [after
stating the nature of the action]— Jennie Jones and Philip Jones, the
above-named plaintiff and defendant, were married during the Great War, in
1916, at Saskatoon, where they lived together for a short time until he went
overseas on active service, returning in 1919. They got along happily until the
summer of 1922. Even after his return, however, he did not support the
plaintiff nor maintain the home. The plaintiff is a stenographer and she
continued at work, the defendant providing enough only to support himself in
the home which she maintained. There is no suggestion of complaint on the wife’s
part until the summer of 1922. They have no children.

[
2
]

His misbehaviour commenced about July, 1922. He began “drinking
and gambling more or less,” as she puts it, away sometimes all night, coming
home late only on her repeated telephone requests. From a date which she fixes
as about September 3, 1922, “there would not be a week in which he was not out
all night, or nearly all night, at least three nights altogether.” On the
evening of November 13, 1922 (he had not been home the previous two nights) he
was going to stay in, but when evening arrived, announced his intention to
attend a “men only party” and went out again. A few minutes later the plaintiff
went out, just for the air apparently, and discovered the defendant’s
automobile on one of the main streets with two women in it, one of whom was the
co-defendant. The ensuing conversation showed that the defendant was then
carrying on “an affair” with the co-defendant. The plaintiff took the key of
the car and put the women out of it. She says she intended to drive herself and
the car into the river. That I am not prepared to accept too seriously. The
husband came along, got another key, and after a scuffle, in which he bruised
her arm and broke her wrist watch, he got control of the car and took the
plaintiff home. She told him that it would be impossible for her to continue to
live with him, and he said he would “get out.” It is to be noted that in this
episode the defendant’s courtesy to the co-defendant was markedly different
from his attitude to his wife.

[
3
]

In April, 1923, there was a reconciliation. He agreed to live as
he should and they lived together until June 3, 1923. He did not, however,
behave himself, and once was arrested for driving his car while drunk.

[
4
]

On this June 3, 1923, when he went out in the evening he
intended, as he stated, to be home by eleven o’clock. At midnight the plaintiff
tried to reach him on the telephone and failed to locate him. At four A.M., she
got up and went out to look for him. After some search, she got into the
co-defendant’s rooms by crawling through a bedroom window, and found her
husband and the co-respondent there in bed together. She is unable or unwilling
to tell very clearly what occurred in this room. She had an altercation with
the co-defendant, in which she was going to hit the co-defendant, and was
restrained by the defendant. In her evidence she said:

He told me to get out of the rooms, and I was not going, and
he said something to the effect that if I didn’t get out or something, and
leave him alone, interfering with him or something to that effect, that he
would kill
me.
I was to stop interfering with his affairs, stop
following him around and interfering with his affairs, or he would kill me,

and he told her also that he was not happy with her. She told
him not to come back home, and shortly afterwards commenced this action. It was
strange that on this important part of her case the plaintiff evidenced such
reluctance and her memory seemed at a loss in giving her evidence. It very much
lessened the value of her testimony.

[
5
]

A police constable deposed that he had often seen the defendant
and the co-defendant together on the streets. About two a.m. on a night in
March. 1923, whilst making an investigation, he discovered them in a bedroom
together. The codefendant was in the bed, and, when in answer to the constable’s
knock, the defendant came to the door, he was only partially clothed,
indicating that he too had been in the bed and had just put on enough clothing
to come to the door. This occasion was during the period of separation, to
which I have already referred.

[
6
]

In the altercation in the co-defendant’s room in June, 1923, the
wife accused the co-defendant of keeping rooms in which to entertain other
women’s husbands, and received the answer, to which no exception was taken by
the husband, that the plaintiff’s husband was keeping the rooms for her.

[
7
]

The plaintiff is a slight woman, inclined to be frail rather than
robust, and it is contended that her health was seriously affected in
consequence of her husband’s conduct. She deposed that she could not keep up
with her work, could not keep her mind on it, could not sleep at nights and
could not eat. Between September and November, 1922, she lost fourteen pounds
in weight. Her employers (an insurance company) have its employees medically
examined once in every year, and in addition to these periodical examinations,
she had consulted the examining physician “in connection with her health on
more than one occasion previous to October 1923,” as he-put it in his
testimony. His evidence is that even before these special consultations he
noted that she was in poor condition, “ a poorer condition of health than when
he had seen her on previous occasions,” and in October, 1923, when she
specially consulted him “she was not exactly sick, she was in poor health,
nervous, not sleeping, thin and anaemic, worried, no one organ gone wrong, just
all round sub-standard,” as the notes read. It was due, in his opinion, to the
mental strain to which she was subjected, and if continued would get worse, and
might shorten her life. In her own evidence she deposed that there was nothing
to cause this condition other than her husband’s conduct. As she gave her
evidence it appeared to me that she lacked what for want of a better
description I have to describe as mental vivacity. There was a slowness of
comprehension at times, and disjointedness in her answers, most unusual in a
woman of her type; nothing at all serious, but noticeable.

[
8
]

It should be noted that there is no suggestion that the husband
was deliberately acting as he did in an intent to injure his wife. It would
seem clear that he must have known that she was put under an unusual mental
strain in consequence of his conduct, and that it was affecting her condition.
In a letter from him written since the action was commenced, his view, that he
did not consider marriage a barrier to his pursuit of pleasure, appears very
clearly, and though I think the plaintiff’s testimony, particularly on the two
outstanding quarrels over the co-defendant, the one on the street and the other
in her rooms must be discounted considerably, still the inference must be drawn
that in spite of consequences, the defendant intended to compel the plaintiff
to submit to his way of living, to use his money to support his mistress,

to
seek his pleasure more or less publicly, notwithstanding the affront to his
wife, whilst his wife was compelled to work to provide the home, He had taken
the part of the mistress in the altercation on the street in June, 1923, and
again in her room in November, 1923. His threat to kill the plaintiff should be
taken
cum grano salis.
It is an indication, however, of his previous
attitude to her, and that for the future she might anticipate a more aggravated
condition of affairs. It indicated a future in which life for the plaintiff, as
the defendant’s wife, could no longer be tolerable, and would be so full of
misery and unhappiness that her health could not stand under it; a breakdown of
some nature would be inevitable, in my opinion.

[
9
]

The question is not, however, whether in my opinion the law
should provide for a dissolution of the marriage, but whether she is entitled
by law to the decree she asks. The practice of the Parliament of Canada has
been to pass a bill dissolving the marriage, under such circumstances, on the
ground of the husband’s adultery; and now in Great Britain it is under
The
Matrimonal Causes Act,
1923, 13 & 14 Geo. V., ch. 19

lawful for any wife to present a petition praying that her
marriage may be dissolved on the ground that her husband has, since the
celebration thereof, and since the passing of this Act, been guilty of
adultery.

[
10
]

This Court must still look to
The Divorce and Matrimonial
Causes Act,
1857, ch. 85, and cannot decree dissolution as against the
husband on finding adultery only.

Adultery coupled with such cruelty as, without adultery would
have entitled her to a divorce
a mensa et thoro,
or of adultery coupled
with desertion, without reasonable excuse, for two years or upwards

has to be established. This plaintiff cannot avail herself of
the latter proviso as to desertion. Shortly after this action was commenced,
the husband abandoned his domicile in Saskatchewan, which was a domicile of
choice, and is now living in the United States. It was conceded that her rights
in this action has to be determined as of the date when the action was
commenced. So to determine the plaintiff’s right we must turn to discover
whether in the law as laid down in the Ecclesiastical Courts of many years ago,
and now interpreted this husband’s conduct can be held to be such cruelty as
would have entitled the wife to a divorce
a mensa et thoro,
“separation
from bed and board.”

[
11
]

I confess that I approach the enquiry as a novice. Matrimonial
causes in Western practice have, until recent years, been rare, and there has
been no opportunity, at least for me, to absorb from practice, the legal lore
surrounding such actions. Now we have a new field, and one in which, from Lord
Herschell’s reference in his speech in
Russell v. Russell
[1897] A.C.
395, at p. 455, 66 L.J..P. 122
, to Lord Brougham’s judgment in
Paterson v.
Paterson,
3 H.L. Cas. 328 (
10 E.R. 120
) when Lord Herschell observed, “and
it is no more than a speculation of Lord Brougham, who cannot be regarded as
specially an authority on the ecclesiastical law,” it would seem that some
supersense is required. This is my apology for the extensive search of the
cases in this judgment, I have made this examination of cases notwithstanding
that it seems well established that decisions on special facts can furnish no
true criteria, as to what is cruelty, using the word in either the popular or
the legal sense, for human beings are never alike. Conduct that may cause pain
and anguish, no less keen because mental, in one person, might little offend
the sensibilities of another person. The character, whether assertive, bold, or
sensitive, the degree of refinement, the physical wellbeing, the condition of
health, mental and bodily, the means of living, position in society, previous
training and such matters, are all relevant to the determination. “What is
tolerable by one may not be by another,” observed Lord Stowell in
D Aguilar
v. D Aguilar,
1 Hagg. Ecc. 773, at p. 782.

[
12
]

Every textbook and every decision takes Lord Stowell’s decision
in
Evans v. Evans,
1 Hagg. Con. 35 (
161 E.R. 466
) as the foundation of
the modern law on the subject of cruelty. And then follow many cases until
1897, when in
Russell v. Russell, supra,
the House of Lords divided five
to four in their views on cruelty. Lord Herschell at p. 457, after an
examination of the cases, summed up the view of the majority, reaffirming
Evans
v. Evans;
“Danger of life, limb, or health, has continued in substance the
rule upon which the Courts have acted.” But as to what conduct will be classed
under this description, even in the judgments of the majority, the language
used is very general and not at all specific.

[
13
]

Evans v. Evans
is the report of a judgment in the
Consistory Court of London, of Sir William Scott, afterwards Lord Stowell. I
have been concerned at the start to discover the nature of the Consistory Court
in which so many of the judgments on this subject were delivered. Its history
and constitution is referred to in the article in 11
Halsbury,
505,
pars. 960
et seq.:

Every archbishop and bishop has a court for the trial of
ecclesiastical causes within his diocese, called the consistory court, * *
which is held by his chancellor as his official principal * * or before his
commissary. * * The chancellor acts in the court as an ordinary or independent
judge, according to ecclesiastical law.

[
14
]

From the Judge Ordinary the appeal was to the delegates, always
Judges, in the Arches Court.

[
15
]

In
Manby v. Scott,
1 Sid. 109, 2 Smith’s L.C., 11 ed. 446,
in the Exchequer Chamber in 1663, which was a suit at law against the husband
for necessaries supplied to the wife, at p. 469, as the translation in Smith’s
L.C. reads, this passage occurs :

2. If the husband will not give necessaries to his wife, she
can make her complaint to the ordinary, and he may give her a remedy; and that
this is the proper course and best adapted to every such complaint is manifest:

First.
Because, common modesty having prohibited such
domestic differences between husband and wife from being unravelled before a
jury, which always hears evidence in public (which can only serve to foment
such internal quarrels, and to render them irreconcilable and irreparable, as
experience too clearly shows), our law provides that the bishop, who is a spiritual
father, should examine the matter with the gravity and learning becoming his
station, and, in discharge of his duty, persuade the husband and wife to
reconciliation. The better to accomplish this, that the
arcana familiae
should
not be made public, the bishop himself, as Bridgman, C.J., said, ought to
examine the matter in private, taking with him his chancellor and his
registrar, and if he cannot bring about a reconciliation he must proceed to
sentence, and this will be according to the demerit of the wife, and not
according to the estate and degree of her husband, as a jury must proceed; for
the latter would be mischievous, since bad wives would have as great provision
as good wives have when the default is on the part of the husband. But in the
spiritual court, such bad wives as have violated their vows shall have such
provision as clerks convict, Stamf. 140; and shall be fed with the bread of
affliction and the water of adversity.

[
16
]

As late as 1854 we find Dr. Lushington in
Chesnutt v.
Chesnutt,
1 Spinks 196 (
164 E.R. 114
) making a reference to attempts to
reconcile the parties and giving judgment only when “called upon to deliver
judgment.” This double function of the Spiritual Court undoubtedly influenced
the decisions. It was easier to perform the duty to reconcile the parties if
the law leaned, even unjustly, against separation or divorce. However the law
as laid down by Lord Stowell in
Evans v. Evans
has never been
challenged. It is difficult to refrain from again quoting it. Subsequent
judgments have invariably started with a reference to it and quotations. My
attention is especially caught by what is stated at E. R. pp. 467, 468, 496,
499. It is too long to quote and the judgment in the E. R. makes reference to
it readily accessible. It was a case of divorce, by reason of cruelty,
instituted by Mrs. Evans. She charged her husband in her libel, as the claim
was then termed, with having been guilty of personal violence of a brutal
character, and many minor matters of aggravation. The facts were found against
her, and Mr. Evans was “exculpated from the charge of unmanly and unlawful
cruelty,” p. 499. Before the examination of the facts proceeded, there is a
most complete and lucid instruction as to the nature of the enquiry. The
importance of the indissolubility of marriage to the happiness of the parties
and the State is stressed. Cruelty releases the duty of cohabitation. Cruelty
is not defined, but negatively certain considerations are excluded from
consideration; such as are not grave and weighty and do not show an absolute
impossibility that the duties of the marriage state can continue to be
discharged. The Court proceeds only on the ground of “danger of life, limb, or
health.”

[
17
]

It is not only interesting to compare the attitude of approach to
the discussion of subjects matrimonal in 1790 with that of 1663. There are many
intermediate causes, until the next great decision in 1897. It has seemed to me
not only interesting but necessary to determine my duty at this date to examine
these intermediate decisions with some care, and pertinent to an appreciation
of
Russell v. Russell.
I have, when on the subject, brought the
examination down to date.

[
18
]

For this purpose, to adopt some system I have made a rough
division of the cases most frequently quoted: (1) Taking those in which the
wife (or husband in some cases) claimed to be in jeopardy from personal
violence; (2) Those in which the question was whether a course of conduct which
did not include adultery amounted to cruelty; and (3) Those cases in which adultery
and other conduct was charged as cruelty.

(1) As to the cases in the first of
these divisions, where the cruelty alleged consisted of personal violence, in
the revision of this judgment my first extended examination thereof has been
eliminated, as the latter divisions are closer to the issues in this action,
Sufficient is it to observe that the charge of Sir C. Creswell to the jury in
Tomkins
v. Tomkins
(1858) 1 Sw. & Tr. 168 (
164 E.R. 678
), is always referred to
for its correct statement :

There must be bodily hurt—not trifling or temporary pain; or a
reasonable apprehension of bodily hurt. It will be for you, on a consideration
of the evidence you have heard, to determine whether the husband has so treated
his wife and so manifested his feelings towards her as to have inflicted bodily
injury, to have caused reasonable apprehension of bodily suffering, or to have
injured health. It is for her to make out the affirmative of what she alleges.

[
19
]

This and other portions of this charge were affirmed as good law
by Lord Herschell in
Russell v. Russell,
at p. 457, in expressing his
view, in which Lords Watson, Macnaghten and Davey concurred. Reference may be
made to:—1630:
Cloborn’s Case,
Hetley 149 (see [1897] A.C. at p. 459);
1790:
Evans v., Evans, supra;
1801:
Oliver v. Oliver,
1 Hagg.
Con. 361 (
161 E.R. 581
) ; 1813:
Harris v. Harris, 2
Hagg. Con. 148 (
161
E.R. 697
) ; 1813:
Waring v. Waring, 2
Hagg. Con. 152 (
161 E.R. 699
);
1826:
Westmeath v. Westmeath, 2
Hagg. Ecc. (supp. 1, 61) (
161 E.R. 992
,
1012); 1831:
Neeld v. Neeld,
4 Hagg. Ecc. 263 (
162 E.R. 1442
) ; 1847:
Saunders
v. Saunders,
1 Rob. Ecc. 549 (
163 E.R. 1131
) ; 1858:
Tomkins v. Tomkins,
supra;
1859:
Curtis v. Curtis, 2
Sw. & Tr. 192 (
164 E.R. 688
),
affirmed 4 Sw. & Tr. 234 (
164 E.R. 1505
) ; 1861:
Smalhvood v. Smalhvood,
2
Sw. & Tr. 398 (
164 E.R. 1050
); 1867:
Forth v. Forth,
36 L.J.P.
122, 16 L.T. 574; 1895:
Mackenzie v. Mackenzie
[1895] A.C. 384
.

[
20
]

And the Canadian cases:—1852 :
Severn v. Severn,
3 Gr.
431
; 1860:
Jackson v. Jackson,
8 Gr. 499
; 1873:
Rodman v. Rodman,
20
Gr. 428
; 1916:
McIlwain v. McIlwain,
35 O.L.R. 533
; 1918:
Bailev v.
Bailey
(Court of Appeal, Ontario, confirming Masten, J.)
1919 CanLII 474 (ON SCAD)
, 45 O.L.R. 59, 48
D.L.R. 750.

[
21
]

In Manitoba:—1908:
Willey v. Willey,
1908 CanLII 265 (MB KB)
, 18 Man. R. 298, 9
W.L.R, 166.

[
22
]

In New Brunswick:—1863 :
Hunter v. Hunter,
10 N.B.R. (5
Allen) 593; 1910:
Currey v. Currey,
1910 CanLII 386 (NB SC)
, 40 N.B.R. 96.

[
23
]

In British Columbia:—1910:
Tims v. Tims,
15 B.C.R. 39, 13
W.L.R. 636
; 1912 :
Edmonds v. Edmonds,
1912 CanLII 1028 (BC CA)
, 17 B.C.R. 282, 1 W W.R. 989, 20
W.L.R. 54; 1914:
Walsh v. Walsh,
1914 CanLII 730 (BC SC)
, 20 B.C.R. 482, 7 W.W.R. 620.

[
24
]

In the North-West Territories:—1896:
Harris v. Harris
(No.
2) (Wetmore, J.)
1906 CanLII 131 (NWT SC)
, 3 Terr. L.R. 416.

[
25
]

In Alberta:—1914:
Lloyd v. Lloyd,
1914 CanLII 671 (AB SCAD)
,
7
Alta. L.R. 307, 6
W.W.R. 1387, 28 W.L.R. 806.

[
26
]

And in Saskatchewan :—1908:
Patrick v. Patrick,
1 Sask. L
R.

44, 7 W.L.R. 470
; 1911:
Maday
v. Maday,
4 Sask. L.R. 18, 16 W.L.R. 701
; 1913:
Moon v. Moon,
1913 CanLII 112 (SKSC)
, 6
Sask. L.R. 41, 3 W.W.R. 856, 23 W.L.R. 153; 1920:
Homunuke v. Homanuke,
1920 CanLII 201 (SK KB)
, 13
Sask. L.R. 186, [1920] 1 W.W.R. 673; and on appeal
1920 CanLII 121 (SK CA)
, 13 Sask. L.R. 557, [1920] 3
W.W.R. 749.

[
27
]

The Saskatchewan decisions were made in actions for alimony,
where the alleged cruelty consisted of actual violence to the person of the
wife, and the rule adopted in these cases was, as it was put by Lamont, J. in
Maday
v. Maday, supra,
to constitute cruelty:

there must be actual violence of such a character as to
endanger personal health or safety or conduct causing a reasonable apprehension
of it.

[
28
]

It might be inferred from what was said in the
Patrick Case,
and
followed in the
Maday Case,
that legal cruelty could consist in law only
in actual violence. The judgments, however, should be read, it seems to me, in
the light of the charges made in these cases, as from the cases to which I will
presently refer it would appear clear that the right to relief is not and never
has been so confined.

(2) The second division cases, in which
conduct, not including physical violence or adultery, was charged as
constituting cruelty, are more pertinent to the present enquiry, and I briefly
note these:

[
29
]

1751:
Leckie v. Leckie,
Elchies’ Dec. H. & W. No. 35,
6 Pat. App. 687, referred to at length in
Russell v. Russell, supra,
at
p. 413 ([1897] A.C.): The House of Lords, Lord Chancellor Hardwicke, delivering
the judgment reversing the Scotch Courts, refused relief to a wife whose
husband had accused her of lasciviousness, representing her to the world as a
monster of nature for lasciviousness and a reproach to her sex. The charge was
made in legal proceedings commenced by her.

[
30
]

1755 :
Holmes v. Holmes, 2
Lee 116 (
161 E.R. 283
), a
decision of Sir George Lee, Chancellor, affirmed in the Arches Court. Personal
violence had been charged as against the husband, but it occurred after a
separation and was not, therefore, taken into account. The husband married the
wife for her money, and lived civilly enough until he got some £2,000 from her.
They quarrelled; she put him into bankruptcy; he absconded and she left him. He
had used abusive language to her. It was held that there was no cruelty
sufficient to entitle her to a divorce. It was not suggested that he had beat
her or put her to any danger while they lived together.

[
31
]

1828:
Bray v. Bray,
1 Hagg. Ecc. 162 (
162 E.R. 543
) : The
judgment is on a motion to strike out a plea in a divorce action. The wife
alleged that the husband had charged her with unchastity and incestuous
intercourse with an uncle, resulting in the birth of a child. It was held
proper as a plea connected with the principal case. Sir John Nicholl at p. 167:

It is not, I think, possible to conceive cruelty of a more
grievous character (except, perhaps great personal violence) than the
accusation made by this husband against his wife.

[
32
]

1850:
Paterson v. Paterson,
3 H.L. Cas. 308 (
10 E.R. 120
).
Neglect, silence, shunning the wife’s company, and declarations that he would
never cohabit with her, were held insufficient to constitute cruelty for which
a divorce
a mensa et thoro
should be decreed. It had not been
established that her health had been affected, or menaced.

[
33
]

1863:
Hudson v. Hudson,
3 Sw. & Tr. 315 (
164 E.R.
1296
). This was a wife’s petition for judicial separation on the ground of
cruelty arid adultery, but the latter charge was not supported and struck out.
Her complaint on the ground of cruelty was that she had suffered much from weak
health and distress of mind, caused to some extent, and, at any rate, increased
by her husband’s conduct. The evidence tendered for her on this branch of the
case was accepted. The burden of her complaint was that the husband was given
to intoxication, used rough and coarse language, was violent and abusive at
times. It was held on the facts that she was in no fear of any actual danger to
her person, and there was no danger of intolerable hardship in her life. When
she separated herself from her husband she did so on a false pretense that she
was leaving on a short visit to a relative, and separated on good terms.

[
34
]

1864:
Pickard v. Pickard,
3 Sw. & Tr. 523, 33 L.J.
Mat. 158. There the husband alleged cruelty by the wife. The wife was
ill-tempered, abusive and guilty of great and unrestrained violence which the
husband had submitted to, adopting, from religious motives, a policy of passive
resistance. She ruled his conduct by threats of personal attack, and when she
had been guilty of assailing him with abuse and blows on the steps of a public
chapel, which he had been attending against her will, and had driven him home
ignominiously, he left her and commenced action. The excitement of the last
attack had induced a fit and much mental and bodily suffering. Whilst the Judge
Ordinary refused to draw the conclusion that his safety was imperilled, or that
he would receive serious bodily harm from her personal violence, as he could
protect himself, the decree was, on the husband making provision for the wife,
granted.

[
35
]

1870:
Kelly v. Kelly,
L.R. 2 P. 59, 39 L.J. Mat. 28: This
was a decision on a wife’s petition for judicial separation on the ground of
cruelty. No actual violence to her person was charged. The husband was a
minister. They had lived together for twenty-eight years when the wife left him
and commenced proceedings. The facts will appear from quotations from the
judgments:

He opened her letters. He called her a vile traitor and
apostate. He told her that no modest woman would associate with her. That she
had given her confidence to another man. He refused to sit at meals with her.
He insisted on occupying a separate bedroom. He told the servants to take

her necessary expenses, * * interdicted against going out at will,

locked in, followed by his servants, and abused in epithets

forbade the house to those who wished to see her, had her letters read before

Her health was imperilled and medical testimony that to expose her further to
such treatment would have led to paralysis or madness was accepted. The husband
was a fanatic, who apparently thought he benefited his wife by thus treating

cruelty, and decree was made for judicial separation.

The conclusion of the Chancellor that this was due to

was concurred in. The argument of the counsel for the defendant

And while it is recognized that violence and personal danger

It will be noted that in some of the Ontario Cases “mental ill
health” is described as “mental distress calculated to endanger her reason.” So
far as I can discover, this way of putting it first occurs in 1905, in
Lovell
v. Lovell, supra,
in the judgment of Moss, C.J.O. It was used there to
describe the result of the defendant’s conduct in that case, and not, as
Ferguson, J.A. in
Bagsham v. Bagshaw
quoted it, as a limitation on the
nature of the mental distress required to be established A similar limitation
is not found in any of the English cases that I have read. The reports do not
show that even in the cases where this language was used there was any argument
on the point. I think I can safely take it that the limitation suggested in the
introduction of this language was accidental, and may disregard it in reaching
a conclusion herein.

Rob. Ecc. 421 (

): Cause

Undoubtedly, the charge of having committed incest is not
per

sufficient to constitute legal cruelty; but, coupled with other

1854:
Chesnutt v. Chesnutt,
1 Spinks 196 (
164 E.R. 114
):
The wife in this case pleaded cruelty and adultery in answer to a suit for
restitution of conjugal rights. I quote from Dr. Lushington’s judgment :

The 3rd article of the allegation pleads that, from five years
after the marriage, Mr. Chesnutt treated his wife with harshness and cruelty,
and particularly during the last two or three years, whilst resident in Church
Terrace, Waterloo Road; that he used obscene and blasphemous language was
constantly intoxicated, and thereby occasioned his wife great mental suffering
and bodily ill health.

Here I must pause and express my doubt whether, if this
article should be proved as laid, the case so stated, according to the legal
interpretation of it, would amount to cruelty, upon proof of which the Court could
decree a separation. Here is no charge either of bodily violence inflicted, or
of threats of personal ill treatment. However disgusting the use of the
language charged, if proved, may be—however degrading habits of
intoxication—however annoying to a wife, especially the wife of a gentleman and
a clergyman—these facts, standing alone, do not constitute legal cruelty. If it
be said that the consequences to the wife are mental suffering and bodily ill
health, I do not think that the case would be carried further. The same might
be said of other vices; of gaming for instance; of gross extravagance, to the
ruin of a wife and family all these might occasion great mental suffering, and,
consequent thereon, bodily ill health to the wife; but they do not constitute
legal cruelty. Such consequences, to be the subject of legal redress, must
emanate from bodily ill treatment) or threats of the same. Such I apprehend to
be the clear line of distinction drawn by all the authorities. * * * * Mental
anxiety, excitement, bodily illness, though occasioned to the wife by the
conduct of the husband, does not constitute cruelty, except such conduct was
accompanied with violence, or threats of violence.

66

Halsbury,

v. Walker

77

is against this view. It is not noticed in the

in

supra,

and the language of Phillimore, L.J. in the

1890:

Wife’s petition for divorce upon the ground of adultery and cruelty. The

The wife complained that she had been delicate all through the married life,

It has been contended before us that he [Butt, J.] was wrong,
that there is evidence of such cruelty as would have entitled the wife to a

The Divorce and Matrimonial Causes Act,
1857,
which empowers a wife to present a petition for dissolution of marriage upon
the ground
(inter alia)
of adultery coupled with such cruelty as without
adultery would have entitled the wife to a divorce
a mensa et thoro.
Whether
that is made out depends upon the effect of the evidence, having regard to the
extent to which it ought to be discounted by reason that in an undefended case
there is no crossexamination of the witnesses, and that leading questions are
often put. I will assume that, making due allowance for all proper discount
upon those grounds, the result of the case is a little on the side of the wife—
that is to say, I will assume that there has been such misconduct on the part
of the husband as to have injured his wife’s health to his knowledge ; and I
will assume that, notwithstanding that knowledge, he continued such misconduct.
If that was the true result of the evidence, I think it would follow that a
case of cruelty had been made out, I do not say that is the true result. I will
assume it.

[
72
]

Lopes, L.J. said at p. 201:

A difficult and important question is raised in this case with
regard to legal cruelty; or rather, I should say, whether what has been proved
in this case amounts to legal cruelty. The suit is an undefended suit, and it
is correct to say that the witnesses have not been cross-examined, and that
many leading questions have been put in examination which in all probability
would not have been put in that form if the suit had been defended It is
therefore not unfair that the evidence should be discounted to a certain
extent. I do not desire to express any opinion whether the facts and the
evidence given raise a case of legal cruelty or not. I am not at all prepared
to say that they do not, if the evidence is to be believed and is not to be
discounted to a very great extent. But I would rather leave a question of this
kind, if it ever arises again, open for decision, without committing myself to
an opinion with regard to it.

allow her to share his bed. He was frequently absent and refused to give an
account of his absences. Once he pushed her from his room so violently that she
fell down. He habitually neglected her and refused to take her out with him,
used violent language and compelled her to do as he wished under threat of
leaving her. He often received letters in ladies’ handwriting, which he refused
to explain, and told her she must live her own life. The continual neglect made
her very ill; she was continually crying, got very thin, and could not eat. Finally
it was discovered that he was keeping a mistress during the whole of the
married life. The medical testimony was to the effect that the husband’s
conduct had injured the wife’s health, and that if continued it would cause
death. The President ( Sir James Hannen) made a decree
nisi
for
dissolution on the ground of adultery and cruelty.

[
74
]

1893:
Walmesley v. Walmesley,
69 L.T. 152, at p. 153, 1 R.
529
: The petitioner and respondent were married in 1889, both being in a good
position. There was no allegation by the wife that her husband had ever treated
her with physical violence, nor even that quarrels or angry words had ever
arisen between them. The cruelty alleged consisted solely of neglect, coldness,
and insults, from which the petitioner’s health had been affected to such an
extent that it was said it would be dangerous for her to continue to live with
the respondent. Within a few days of the marriage the latter refused to occupy
the same bedroom with her, never went anywhere with her, and ceased to speak to
her unless an answer became absolutely necessary. When their child was born he
took no notice of it, and refused to allow it to be christened after him. He
declined to take things from his wife’s hands, and, in one house where they
were stopping, rather than eat his meals with her, he took them in the kitchen.
On one occasion he said to a lady, in his wife’s presence, that the best way to
treat a wife was to tie her to a bedpost and keep her there. She suffered great
mental agony from his treatment, which told upon her appearance, and at length
her health quite gave way. A doctor who attended her was of opinion that, if
subjected to a longer continuation of this course of ill-treatment, she would
develop melancholia. In 1892 she first learned of the respondent’s relations
with another woman, and eventually instituted these proceedings. Barnes, J.,
held following
Bethune v. Bethune
and
Kelly v. Kelly, supra,
cruelty
as well as adultery established, and “therefore” pronounced decree
nisi.

[
75
]

1895:
Mackenzie v. Mackenzie
[1895] A.C. 384, 22 Rethe 32
:
The question for decision here was whether the wife had reasonable excuse for
separating from her husband. The only actual personal violence occurred in an
altercation over their child, when the husband gripped his wife’s hand with
considerable force unjustifiably to restrain her, and take the child away from
her. Considerable violence was used on this occasion, but it did not result in
any serious consequences. Ths husband, as it was found, had taken care to inform
himself of his legal rights and regarded them as duties to perform or maintain,
notwithstanding the pain that might be inflicted on his wife and required her
to bend her will to his and submit absolutely to his wishes. When the wife was
ordered South for her health, he unjustifiably refused to let her take her few
months old baby with her, refusing to trust the child with her. He used a
threat to separate her from the child to compel her submission, and had
threatened to put her under lock and key, and expressed his regret that he had
not done so before. The House of Lords reached the conclusion on the facts that
the wife could not have returned without apprehension of actual violence from
the husband, and held that she had just cause for separation.

[
76
]

1896:
Le Couteur v. he Couteur,
reported only in
The
Times,
March 2,. 1896, in a note to
Gwynne Hall on Divorce,
386, and
referred to in
Dorsett v. Dorsett
1921 CanLII 712 (MB KB)
, [1921] 1 W.W.R. 708, by Mathers,
C.J.K.B., at p. 718:

The husband had persisted in treating his wife as a menial and
putting her in a subordinate position while openly carrying on an adulterous
intercourse with another woman in the family residence, and had threatened that
if she made any fuss he would go abroad with the woman. In consequence of this
treatment the wife became ill, both physically and mentally. The Court
following
Kelly v. Kelly,
L.R. 2 P. 31, 39 L.J. Mat. 28, said the wife
had been exposed to insults of the worst kind which, having caused a breakdown
of her health, was cruelty of a very gross kind.

[
77
]

1901:
Thompson v. Thompson,
85 L.T. 172, Jeune, P.: The
headnote reads:

If the conduct of the husband is such as to cause a breakdown
of the health of the wife, by reason of the disgrace and shock arising out of a
conviction of the husband under
The Criminal Law Amendment Act,
1885 (48
& 49 Vict., ch. 69), the court will hold this to constitute legal cruelty
on the part of the husband, and will grant a decree
nisi
to the wife,
the adultery having also been proved.

[
78
]

The husband, who took holy orders after his marriage, while a
curate, indulged in familiarities with various young girls, took two of them
into his service in spite of his wife’s remonstrances, and was convicted under
sec. 5, subsec. 1 of
The Criminal Law Amendment Act,
and sentenced to
twelve months’ hard labour. The result of his course of conduct was utterly to
shatter the health of the petitioner, who was now a mere shadow of her former
self. The President (without reported comment) held the cruelty to be
established, and granted a decree
nisi.

[
79
]

1903 :
Jeapes v. Jeapes,
89 L.T. 74: Suit by husband for
dissolution of marriage on ground of wife’s adultery. Wife denied, and asked
for dissolution on grounds of adultery and cruelty. The headnote reads:

A husband left his wife and children without any means of
support, and afterwards filed a petition against his wife for a dissolution of
his marriage on the ground of her adultery, alleging that she had given birth
to a child after he had left her, of which he was not the father. Upon proof
being given that the allegation had had the effect of injuring the health of
the wife, it was held that such conduct on the part of the husband constituted
legal cruelty so as to entitle the wife to relief.

[
80
]

The doctor who attended the respondent in her confinement said he
found her in very depressed condition. He had no doubt that condition was
entirely due to desertion of her husband and to the threats he had used against
her. The President (Sir Francis Jeune):

Upon the whole I am of opinion that the charge of cruelty
against the husband has been made out. To leave a wife to starve is undoubted
cruelty, but I was not certain whether it could be construed into legal
cruelty. However, when one considers the false charge made, and the neglect of
the wife in leaving her unprovided for, which have had the effect of impairing
her health, I think I may find that such conduct does constitute legal cruelty.
Since the charges of adultery and cruelty against the husband are established,
I dismiss his petition with costs, and pronounce a decree
nisi
in favour
of the wife, with costs, and give her the custody of her three children.

[
81
]

1919:
Baker v. Baker
(referred to by Mathers, C.J.K.B., at
p. 71.3 [1921] 1 W.W.R.) reported in
The London Times,
December 11,
1919: Petition for dissolution on the ground of adultery and cruelty. Cruelty
was denied. Petitioner was a theatrical singer and the cruelty consisted in
persistently writing letters to her containing threats to commit suicide when
she was about to perform at the theatre. The letters had a serious effect on
her health. They were manifestly written to cause her annoyance and mental
anguish, a course of conduct which was cruel and which, in fact, injured her
health. The decree was granted.

[
82
]

The only Canadian cases I have been able to discover under this
heading are:

[
83
]

1879:
Howey v. Howey,
27
Gr. 57
: A husband locked his wife
out in consequence of her going on a visit against his3 orders. Held by
Spragge, C, such an act of exclusion and expulsion as entitled her to alimony,
when the husband afterwards lived in adulterous intercourse with a woman in his
own house in a way that rendered that house an unfit place for the habitation
of the wife. It was suggested also that adultery on the part of the husband
alone was sufficient ground for alimony.

[
84
]

1891:
Aldrich v. Aldrich,
21 O.R. 447
: Boyd, C. held that
a woman in law and in morals is justified in leaving and in refusing to return
to a husband who had committed adultery; but his act which breaks up the
household does not relieve him from his duty to maintain her; and proof of that
offence would be sufficient upon which to award alimony.

[
85
]

1914:
Walsh v. Walsh
,
1914 CanLII 730 (BC SC)
, 20 B.C.R. 482, 7 W.W.R. 620:
Petition for divorce on the ground of adultery and cruelty. Adultery was
proved, but the wife failed to establish cruelty. It was shown that the husband
slept with a razor and sharp knife under his pillow, that on the wife
discovering it and asking him what it was for, he said to protect himself, and
on her then enquiring what he wanted to protect himself from, he answered that
he thought she might do some harm to him when he was sleeping. This made her
nervous and she made him take another room. Irving, J. held that her safety was
not compromised, nor any fears for it entertained by her, and that the husband
could not be found guilty of legal cruelty unless he had either inflicted
bodily injury upon her or so conducted himself as to cause actual injury to her
mental or bodily health, and thus have rendered future cohabitation more or
less dangerous.

[
86
]

1919:
B. v. B.,
1919 CanLII 620 (AB SCTD)
, [1919] 3 W.W.R. 894, a decision of Scott,
J. in a proceeding for divorce on the ground of adultery coupled with cruelty.
The adultery was proved. The only evidence of cruelty offered was to the effect
that about seven or eight years before the adultery had been committed, the
husband, coming home one night under the influence of liquor, had called his
wife “terrible names” in front of others. She had, notwithstanding, continued
to live with him, and there is not in the case any suggestion that her health
had been impaired.

[
87
]

1921:
Dorsett v. Dorsett

1921 CanLII 712 (MB KB)
, [1921] 1 W.W.R. 708: Wife’s
petition for divorce for adultery and cruelty. The husband and wife separated
under agreement and husband had been living with another woman. In the
temporary absence of this woman, on the wife taking ill, she was brought to the
husband’s residence, and whilst she was there the other woman returned and the
adulterous relations were resumed in the same house. Mathers, C.J.K.B. held
that though this constituted cruelty in the popular sense, it was not cruelty
in the legal sense. “The petitioner’s health was not impaired by it and
therefore it lacked cruelty in the legal sense.” Divorce refused but decree of
judicial separation granted. It would seem doubtful if this decision would now
be followed in Manitoba (see Dennistoun, J.A. in
Newton v. Newton,
1924 CanLII 350 (MB CA)
, 34
Man. R. 190, [1924] 2 W.W.R. 840, at p. 848, [1924] 3 D.L.R. 887).

[
88
]

This chronological notation of cases seems to me to point
conclusively to a breaking away in all the Courts from the rigour of the
decisions in the Ecclesiastical Courts. Lord Stowell stated in 1790
(Evans
v. Evans, supra,
at p. 38 [1 Hagg. Con.]).

And if it be complained that by this inactivity of the Courts
much injustice may be suffered, and much misery produced, the answer is that
Courts of Justice do not pretend to furnish cures for all the miseries of human
life, * * They cannot make men virtuous.

[
89
]

Accepting this in its totality, nevertheless from the more recent
cases a desire to save the wife from misery and injustice is given greater
prominence in the actual decisions upon the facts, and granting as well that
the general happiness of the married life is secured by its indissolubility
(Lord Stowell at p. 38 [1 Hagg. Con.]) the advisability of too stiff an
application thereof is much lessened in this day of grace, by the general
alteration in the status of women since 1790. Now she has other careers open to
her besides marriage, and is not driven to the only venture open to a woman in
1790.

[
90
]

The statutory law of 1857 brought into force in the Territories
in 1870, will not permit a decree for dissolution of marriage on the ground of
adultery alone, on the part of the husband, no matter how profligate. There
must be desertion for upwards of two years or cruelty, “but not necessarily
cruelty which would support a sentence
propter saevitiam,”
and in those
cases in which it was established that the husband’s adultery was committed in
such a shocking way or accompanied by other misconduct, that the wife was put
in misery and her health affected, bodily or mentally, in consequence thereof,
it will be found that the decree for dissolution was always made, if prayed
for. It must be borne in mind too that we now have a better understanding of
the effect of misery and pain and anguish of mind in its relation to health,
and no Court feels itself bound on questions of fact, by the limited
acquaintance of earlier times with what is now common knowledge. The finding of
fact as to whether the wife’s health was injured, or is menaced, must be made
on the common knowledge of today, each case being considered on its own special
facts.

[
91
]

I have to grant that to decree dissolution in this case may be to
go somewhat farther than would appear upon the facts to have been done in any
previous decision, and would seem to be at variance with the dicta I have
quoted from Dr. Lushington’s judgment in 1854 in
Chesnutt v. Chesnutt,
1
Spinks 196. The, nearest case in point of fact is
Beauclerk v. Beauclerk,
supra,
where the husband lived with successive mistresses, diverted
luxuries to them, told his wife of his infidelities and of his preference of
them to her, and her health was affected in consequence of the anguish of mind
occasioned. I have already intimated that this defendant must have known that
plaintiff’s health was affected by his conduct, and continued and was prepared
to still continue, even when the full extent of it was discovered,
notwithstanding such knowledge. So that if we substitute for Beauclerk’s
successive mistresses, the same mistresses at different times, for the
diversion of luxuries, the letting the plaintiff earn her own living, and even
partly support the defendant, whilst he diverted his earnings to the keep of
the mistress, and instead of telling the plaintiff of his infidelities and
preference for his mistress, a course of conduct that but lightly concealed the
former, and plainly showed the latter, it would seem to me that Mrs. Beauclerk
fared no worse than the plaintiff. And whilst fully appreciating that what was
said in the
Beauclerk Case
was merely dicta, I am confident that it is
in accord with what was said and decided in the many cases to which I have
referred, and I feel no disposition to find fault with anything wherein I can
find a warrant for granting to the plaintiff the relief she seeks from a
marriage which to her was intolerable, and would be to any decent woman. There
will be decree
nisi,
for dissolution after six months have elapsed.
Leave to apply for alimony again, if desired. Costs to plaintiff.

Decree nisi with costs.
